channel.description: Aggregated headlines linking to original publishers

item.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
item.description: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function and increase the risk of hospitalization and premature death. Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.

item.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
item.description: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

item.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
item.description: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

item.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
item.description: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

item.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
item.description: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

item.title: Georgia’s Pecan Belt
item.description: Since an early-1900s planting boom, orchards along the Flint River in southwest Georgia have become a center of U.S. pecan production.

item.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
item.description: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

item.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
item.description: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

item.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
item.description: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
item.description: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

item.title: A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03718-4 Potent immune responses against diverse HIV strains have ignited the field, but major hurdles remain.

item.title: The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03809-2 Generic versions of an effective HIV drug have been approved, and an HIV vaccine is on the horizon. Now is no time for funders to take their foot off the pedal.

item.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
item.description: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

item.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
item.description: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

item.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
item.description: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory […]

item.description: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft. The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a […]

First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan’s surface at multiple scales during […]

item.title: NASA Hubble’s New View of NGC 4394 Raises the Bar
item.description: The brilliant galaxy NGC 4394 with its distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this Hubble Space Telescope image

item.title: A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange form of magnetism in an ordinary-looking metal that has no overall magnetization yet profoundly changes how electrons behave. The breakthrough offers a promising new path toward understanding exotic quantum materials and developing future electronic technologies.

item.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
item.description: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

item.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
item.description: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

item.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
item.description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

item.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
item.description: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

item.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

item.title: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
item.description: IBM and University of Chicago researchers have demonstrated that a quantum computer can complete an extraordinarily complex calculation in just 15 minutes, beyond the practical reach of leading classical computing methods. A novel error-detection technique also allows scientists to establish confidence in the accuracy of the results, overcoming a major hurdle in quantum computing.

item.title: America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn
item.description: America’s power grid is falling dangerously behind as electricity demand skyrockets, fueled by data centers, electric vehicles, and industry. The U.S. is building only 10% of the new high-voltage transmission lines experts say it needs, threatening higher energy prices and greater blackout risks. Researchers argue that political obstacles and outdated regulations, rather than technological limitations, are the real problem.

item.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
item.description: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

item.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
item.description: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.

item.title: Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures
item.description: Scientists have developed remarkable materials that can crawl, walk, and dig using their own internal energy, potentially paving the way for a new generation of autonomous soft robots. They also discovered that making individual components more active can paradoxically make the entire material less responsive, challenging a long-standing principle of engineering.

item.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
item.description: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

item.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

item.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
item.description: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

item.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
item.description: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

item.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
item.description: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.

item.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
item.description: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

item.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
item.description: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

item.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
item.description: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

item.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

item.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
item.description: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
item.description: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

item.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
item.description: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

item.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
item.description: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

item.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.

item.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
item.description: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

item.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

item.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
item.description: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision
item.description: Scientists have discovered a new genetic eye disease that can silently damage peripheral and night vision while leaving central sight largely unaffected for years. The condition may be detectable through an unusual difficulty adjusting to darkness, offering a potential early warning sign before irreversible retinal damage occurs.

item.title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis
item.description: Scientists have developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a major study involving nearly 70,000 patients. By revealing subtle patterns that conventional screening misses, the technology could help doctors detect cancer earlier and spare patients unnecessary invasive procedures.

item.title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
item.description: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.

item.title: A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a common blood pressure drug can activate calorie-burning brown fat in mice, potentially opening a new path toward improving metabolic health. An analysis of more than 100,000 patients also revealed surprising links between brown fat and lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, anxiety, and depression.

item.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
item.description: AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

item.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
item.description: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

item.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
item.description: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

item.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
item.description: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

item.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
item.description: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

item.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
item.description: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

item.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
item.description: Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.

item.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
item.description: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

item.title: A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet
item.description: A promising material for ultra-fast optical communications has held a secret for decades, but scientists may have finally cracked it. Researchers at KAIST and Caltech have precisely measured how barium titanate controls and absorbs light, resolving longstanding uncertainties that have slowed its development. Their findings could make it easier to build optical devices that transmit information faster while wasting less light.

item.title: BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey
item.description: Nature, Published online: 21 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03803-8 European and Japanese probes will trace different paths around the planet to study its surface and its surroundings.

item.title: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry
item.description: A surprising discovery at Brown University is challenging one of chemistry's most fundamental textbook explanations. Researchers found direct evidence that Einstein's theory of relativity changes how heavy atoms form triple bonds, causing normally distinct types of chemical bonds to blend together. The breakthrough confirms a decades-old prediction and suggests that traditional chemistry rules don't fully apply to heavy elements such as bismuth.

item.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

item.title: NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test
item.description: NASA has successfully tested a powerful RS-25 rocket engine, firing it for 200 seconds to gather data that could make future Moon missions safer and more reliable. The test supports preparations for the 2028 Artemis IV Moon landing and NASA’s ultimate ambition of sending astronauts to Mars.

item.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
item.description: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

item.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
item.description: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

item.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
item.description: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

item.title: For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard
item.description: A study of more than 10,000 college students found that exercising regularly may be more important for mental health than pushing yourself through intense or lengthy workouts. Students who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety a year later, suggesting that consistency could be a key ingredient in protecting mental well-being.

item.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
item.description: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.
